answer: Hamas and other armed groups are accused of operating among civilians in Gaza. UN bodies documented weapons in vacant UN schools in 2014 and 2020; in this war they report only allegations. The UN human rights office said Israel's army mostly did not substantiate its human-shield claims about hospitals and schools, and could not verify them. The army's claim about tunnels under UNRWA's headquarters is unverified. The ICRC says the duty to respect the laws of war does not depend on reciprocity, so a defender's violations do not release the attacker. A UN commission found that Israel's use of heavy weapons was an intentional attack on civilians, and the UN human rights office found repeated violations in six strikes; Israel rejects both. Our reading: the UN has documented more about Israeli strikes than about Hamas's use of civilian areas; each strike must be judged on its own facts.

facts.text: The laws of war bind the attacker whatever the defender does. Israel is not a party to Additional Protocol I, but the UN human rights office notes that it accepts that some of its provisions reflect customary law. The ICRC's customary-law study lists, as rules for all parties, the prohibition on human shields (Rule 97), the duty to take precautions to spare civilians (Rule 15), and the rule that respect for the law does not depend on reciprocity (Rule 140). Protocol I itself says a violation of the human-shield prohibition does not release the other party from its obligations to civilians. The United States is not a party to Additional Protocol I either; its Defense Department Law of War Manual says it supports the customary principle behind some provisions, but not necessarily as the protocol words them.

could_not_verify: I looked for findings by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty or the UN Commission that Hamas used human shields in the 2023-2026 war and found only the UN human rights office's reports of 'allegations'. For the 2014 war the independent record is the UN Secretary-General's and UNRWA's own statements; the Amnesty and Human Rights Watch statements on that war are advocacy sources and are not counted.
The Israeli army's claim about the tunnels under UNRWA's headquarters was not independently verified in any source I could read; UNRWA said it did not know what was beneath the site.
The NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence report on Hamas and human shields could not be read; it appears only as quoted by Lawfare, so I did not use it as a source.
I did not read the Israeli army's own investigations of individual strikes, or the Israeli mission's own statements.

Facts 1 and 2: I found no outlet that reports the report's paragraph on the army's human-shield statements (paragraph 22), so what the UN human rights office said about the army's evidence rests on the report itself plus the Reuters and AP reports of the army's own claims; that assessment is single-sourced. Only the UN's press release and AFP (Gulf News) repeat the report's line about Palestinian armed groups' conduct; the co-location sentence has only the report (UPI quotes it but its page could not be fetched). LBC was removed because its page misstates the UN's view.
Fact 7 (the 19 June 2024 report): the UN human rights office and UN News are one organisation, AFP, JusticeInfo and Daily Sabah are one wire; Democracy Now is a separate report of the same content.
Fact 8: the report's own words are quoted; Al Jazeera and CBC (Reuters) report the same figures. News reports differ on the period the 8,119 covers; the report says verified by 2 September 2024.
Fact 9: Israel's rejections each have one or two sources (AFP, Reuters, Al Jazeera, UN News); I did not read the Israeli mission's own statements.
The US position on Additional Protocol I is sourced to the Defense Department's Law of War Manual; I did not read the State Department's own statements on which provisions it treats as customary.
not_claimed: This card does not say that Israel targets civilians, and does not say it does not; that is contested and has to be judged strike by strike.
It does not say that Hamas's conduct justifies civilian deaths or removes the attacker's duties.
It does not say that every report of Hamas operating from civilian places has been verified; some are allegations.
It does not say any particular strike was lawful or unlawful.

skeptic.notes: Round 3: checked the OHCHR report itself: para 22 says the IDF released more than 27 statements on Al-Shifa alleging human-shield use and that in most instances it did not offer substantial evidence; OHCHR could not verify them. That context is hospitals and schools, so I narrowed the answer to 'about hospitals and schools'. Para on proportionality ('raise further concerns that ... violated the principle of proportionality') matches fact 7. Customary-law basis (ICRC Rules 15, 97, 140; OHCHR noting Israel accepts some AP I provisions as customary) fixes fact 3; the US position is still not sourced. Still short, so not verified: [must-fix] fact 1 (human-shield evidence in this war): OHCHR report is the record, read first-hand; the only other source (Reuters) covers the army's claim, not the report: add a second reader of OHCHR's paragraph 22, or split the army's claim into its own fact and record-flag the OHCHR one. [must-fix] fact 7 (OHCHR six-month report): record read; only Al Jazeera reads it; add e.g. CBC/Reuters https://amp.cbc.ca/lite/story/1.7377967 (cited on fact 8) as a second reader and set record true. Fact 6 passes the gate with UN twice and AFP twice, i.e. two origins: [should-fix] add an independent report of the 19 June 2024 report. [nit] the six-strike rejection (fact 8) is one AFP text. The answer leans on fact 1 (short), so it cannot be verified. 'Our reading' sentence: 'the UN has documented more about Israeli strikes than about Hamas's use of civilian areas' states what has been documented, not what happened, labelled as the authors' reading per docs/chapters.md; I judge it fair to both directions and carried by facts 0, 1, 5, 6.
